title.narrative: NIHR Development Awards Call 1: A UK-South Asia Collaborative to address the impact of maternal micronutrient deficiencies on infant-neurodevelopment

description.narrative: A low-and-middle-income country (LMIC) award led by the Sitaram Bhartia Institute of Science and Research in India working in collaboration with partners based in Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka and key stakeholders across the health, policy and non-governmental organisation sector to understand how a lack of vitamins and minerals (micronutrients) in mothers and babies affects children's brain development and how it can be prevented and/or treated. Vitamins and minerals are critical for maintaining health at all stages of life. Despite recent efforts to support children's growth, the problem of inadequate micronutrient intake among mothers and infants remains prevalent and under emphasised in LMICs, particularly within the most impoverished communities. Data indicates that deficiencies in certain micronutrients, such as Vitamin B-12, Vitamin D, or iron, can adversely affect a child's brain development. However, there is insufficient research on effective strategies to address these within LMICs. Addressing these gaps in knowledge is critical to preventing children in poorer communities from being left behind, perpetuating a cycle of inequality. The award explores key research questions aimed at addressing how the needed micronutrients can best be provided, whether the focus should be on single nutrients or multiple nutrients at once, and increasing the understanding of how restrictive diets during pregnancy affect micronutrient levels. Additional consideration will be given to whether to supplement mothers, babies, or both, determining the most appropriate doses and duration for identified supplements, and identifying and screening risk factors during pregnancy. The award will involve a detailed review of existing research on the impact of micronutrient deficiencies on children's brain development, coupled with interviews, home environment assessments, and blood tests of a few mother-infant pairs from four countries. Current policies will form the basis of activities focused on the identification of potential enhancements, the arrangement of workshops to assess the efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of proposed interventions which will be used to develop and refine a multicentric intervention plan along with identification and assessment of potential study sites. At the same time, the training and development of skills in South Asian partner countries will take place to build local capacity. The research team will work with government health administrations across South Asia to develop an evidence-based public health intervention plan, based on the tested interventions.

The award has four objectives: 1. To develop a multi-disciplinary partnership involving nutrition, maternal and child health and public health expertise in India, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. 2. To develop an understanding of key maternal micronutrient deficiencies and their impact on infant neurodevelopment. 3. To evaluate the national health policy framework of identified South Asian countries and propose a mitigation plan for addressing maternal micronutrient deficiencies. 4. To identify key research areas and to understand the feasibility of such work in the field including potential study sites and the ethics/data governance frameworks.
